job.style: a news-style report about a real-world situation

response.passage: In a recent digital infrastructure update, engineers highlighted how our global connectivity functions. While we often use Wi-Fi to connect our devices at home, this is merely a local wireless link to a router, which then connects to an Internet Service Provider (ISP) through physical cables. Many people mistakenly believe the internet is entirely wireless, but the vast majority of global data travels through massive fiber-optic cables laid deep under the ocean. These cables use pulses of light, not electricity, to carry data across continents at incredible speeds. When you send a photo to a friend, it is not transmitted as one single block. Instead, the file is broken down into tiny, manageable pieces called packets. These packets travel independently across various paths through the network and are reassembled by the receiving device. Furthermore, every device connected to this network, including your smart refrigerator or CCTV camera, is assigned a unique IP address to ensure data reaches the correct destination. Finally, when you upload files to the cloud, they are not stored in a magical space in the sky. They are actually saved on physical, high-performance servers located in secure data centers on the ground, which require constant maintenance and electricity to operate.
response.summary: The internet relies on a complex network of physical cables and servers rather than wireless magic. Data is broken into packets for transmission, and every connected device requires a unique address to function.
